content: A study was conducted in three hyperendemic villages in India to evaluate the diagnostic and treatment approaches for leprosy. The study included all patients, their household contacts, and neighbors, with a total sample size of 3,287 participants. The primary objective was to determine whether a diagnostic test with sufficient sensitivity and specificity could identify Mycobacterium leprae infection (latent leprosy) among contacts and whether its use was feasible under programmatic conditions. Between March and October 2011, serological tests were performed, and all seropositive individuals, along with a randomly selected subset of seronegative individuals, were invited for dermatological examinations between December 2011 and March 2012. Diagnosis was based on the presence of hypopigmented, anesthetic lesions, slit-skin smears (SSS), and evaluations by leprosy specialists. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, confirmation was achieved through biopsy and further review. The diagnostic tests demonstrated high sensitivity (89% and 87%) for confirming cases but had low specificity (42% and 39%). A systematic review was conducted to assess the effectiveness and safety of a single uniform multidrug therapy (U-MDT) regimen for all leprosy cases compared to the current standard regimens. The standard regimens include a 12-month three-drug combination for multibacillary (MB) leprosy and a six-month two-drug combination for paucibacillary (PB) leprosy. The U-MDT regimen consists of a six-month course of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for both MB and PB leprosy patients. The literature review included studies published between 1996 and January 2017, with no language restrictions. The search strategy utilized MeSH terms and text words related to leprosy and treatment regimens, and additional studies were identified through reference lists. A total of 34 citations were retrieved, and 12 studies met the inclusion criteria. These studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials, and observational studies comparing U-MDT with the standard regimens. The evidence synthesis revealed that U-MDT was comparable to the standard regimens in terms of clinical, histological, and bacteriological improvement or cure. There was no significant difference in relapse rates, leprosy reactions, disability progression, or the rate of decrease in the bacterial index. However, the quality of the included studies was moderate to low, with a high risk of bias and serious imprecision in some estimates. Meta-analysis was not conducted due to the limited number of high-quality RCTs. Adverse events associated with U-MDT were assessed in several studies. Common side effects included cutaneous pigmentation, xeroderma, abdominal pain, and nausea. Patient satisfaction with U-MDT was generally high, although some participants expressed concerns about skin discoloration. The dropout rates and follow-up durations varied across studies, with some reporting losses to follow-up. In conclusion, while U-MDT appears to be a feasible and effective alternative to the standard regimens for leprosy treatment, further high-quality research is needed to confirm its long-term safety and efficacy. The findings have implications for national leprosy control programs, particularly in resource-limited settings.
